To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified a transcription factor network that represses CF gene expression in airways.
we used an siRNA screen in Calu-1 lung epithelial cells to identify nearly 40 transcription factors that repress CFTR gene expression.
we have identified a network of repressor TFs recruited to a CFTR enhancer element in airway epithelia that suppresses CFTR gene expression and that depletion of these factors improves CFTR function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the transcriptional mechanisms that regulate CFTR expression and the identification of new therapeutic targets to increase CFTR production in the airway.
the transcriptional control of CFTR in the airway, a key determinant of the pathophysiology of cystic fibrosis.
the molecular mechanisms that control CFTR expression and function in the airway and identifies novel therapeutic targets to increase CFTR production and improve CFTR function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a network of TFs represses CF expression in the airway, with Klf5 and Etsh being the strongest repressing factors.
the CFTR gene is repressed in the airway and that this is mediated through the recruitment of repressors to a specific cis-regulatory element, the -35 kb enhancer.
a transcription factor network repressed the CFTR locus and this was overcome by depletion of Krüppel like 5 (KLF5) and Ets homology factor (EHF).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the low abundance of the CFTR gene in the airway is due to the presence of a repressive transcription factor network.
the low CFTR expression levels in airway epithelians are due to the recruitment of a transcriptional network of repressive factors to the locus.

we have identified novel transcriptional regulators of CFTR expression that are recruited to the airway-specific CFTR promoter, and their depletion increases the levels of CFTR in lung epithelial cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CFTR expression is repressed by several transcription factors, and that these repressors may be potential targets for therapeutic enhancement of the CFTR gene.
the airway epithelial expression of CFTR is repressed by a network of TFs that are recruited to a specific enhancer.
the low levels of CFTR in the airway are not due to the absence of activating enhancers, but to the presence of repressive factors.
